A focal study of the Southern little yellow-eared bat, Vampyressa pusilla, has clarified several key life-history parameters for this small phyllostomid. Neonates emerge with a remarkably modest body mass of 3 grams [Wwb = 3 grams], a value estimated from comparative scaling relationships with the larger congener Sturnira lilium. The adult ultimate body weight, which serves as the target size for somatic growth, is approximately 13 grams [Wwi = approximately 13 grams], placing this species among the smallest of the stenodermatine fruit bats. Under the stable thermal conditions found within Neotropical roost cavities, which average 37 °C [T = 37 °C], the resting metabolic rate reaches a maximum of 18.6 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 18.6 milliliters of oxygen per hour], a relatively low value that aligns with the energy-conserving physiology typical of small frugivorous bats.

Reproductive timing in Vampyressa pusilla is closely tied to the thermoregulatory demands of gestation and lactation. The gestation period extends for 105 days [tg = 105 days] when females maintain a core body temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C], a duration that is typical for a bat of this body size. Following parturition, the nutritional dependence of the pup is relatively prolonged; the time since birth at weaning spans 30.5 days since birth [tx = 30.5 days since birth] under the same thermal regime. At the point of weaning, the young animal weighs roughly 9 grams [Wwx = roughly 9 grams], reflecting substantial growth from the neonatal stage but still considerably less than the adult mass. This extended period of maternal investment is energetically demanding, as the lactating female must substantially increase her daily food intake to sustain both herself and her rapidly growing offspring.

Sexual maturation in this species is a notably protracted process relative to its small body size. Individuals do not attain reproductive competence until approximately 289 days since birth [tp = approximately 289 days since birth] when maintained at a core temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C]. This extended juvenile phase stands in contrast to the rapid maturation observed in many other small mammals and may reflect the high energetic costs associated with developing the cognitive and sensory capacities necessary for navigating complex forest understories and locating patchily distributed fruit resources. The maximum lifespan recorded for this species, also measured under captive conditions at 37 °C [T = 37 °C], is approximately 4,380 days [am = approximately 4,380 days], which translates to exactly 12 years and is an exceptionally long life for a placental mammal of only 13 grams adult body mass.

The reproductive rate of Vampyressa pusilla is, as expected for a long-lived, small-bodied bat, quite low. Females produce a single pup per litter [N_R_i = single pup per litter], and they typically complete this reproductive event only once each year, yielding an annual fecundity of one offspring per year [Ri = one offspring per year]. This slow pace of reproduction, combined with the substantial energetic investment in a single, large-bodied neonate, aligns with the classic life-history syndrome of a "slow" species. The trade-off is evident when one considers that the weaning mass of 9 grams [Wwx = 9 grams] represents roughly 69 percent of the ultimate adult body weight of 13 grams [Wwi = 13 grams], demonstrating that the mother must provision her single offspring to a remarkably advanced developmental stage before nutritional independence is achieved.

Finally, understanding the ecological niche of Vampyressa pusilla contextualizes its measured physiological traits. As a primarily frugivorous gleaner foraging within dense forest undergrowth, this species relies heavily on the spatial memory of productive fruit patches. The long maturation time of 289 days since birth [tp = 289 days since birth] at puberty likely allows for the development of the hippocampal and neocortical regions necessary for this cognitive task at a temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C]. The maximum longevity of 4,380 days [am = 4,380 days] is a further hallmark of this slow life-history strategy; such extended lifespans in small bodied mammals are typically associated with a low extrinsic mortality rate, which for this bat is likely afforded by its use of well-concealed diurnal roosts and its relatively low exposure to aerial predators at a temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C]. The species thus illustrates a beautifully coherent life-history package, where a low reproductive output, extended development, and exceptional longevity are all functionally integrated with its specific ecological demands.
